title: “Years of Experience”: What Kind?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Setting aside the policy debate over pay scales, Stuart asks teachers and hiring committees to think more carefully about what 'years of experience' actually signifies. He argues the term is a blunt instrument, since eleven years can mean growing cynicism, indiscriminate fad-chasing or deliberate improvement. He warns that younger teachers tend to undervalue experience and older teachers overvalue it, and proposes judging colleagues by the results their work produces. Those results should be wide-angle: academic, motivational and social-emotional. The piece ends by turning the question inward, asking what kind of experience each teacher is building today, and answering that warm self-critique and focused pursuit of excellence are what make years count.
points: 'Years of experience' is a blunt instrument that conceals very different career trajectories, from cynical coasting to indiscriminate chasing of every initiative.
Both age cohorts carry bias: younger teachers undervalue experience while older teachers overvalue it.
The fairer standard is results, defined broadly to include academic, motivational and social-emotional outcomes.
Experience only compounds into expertise when it is paired with aggressive learning from mistakes.
quotes: First, “years of experience” is a blunt instrument. There is a huge difference between a teacher with 11 years of experience who has become increasingly cynical and increasingly adept at doing as little as possible, and a teacher who has spent 11 years working slavishly at All the Things, saying yes to everything with no discernment and constantly chasing after the latest new fad.
Second, beware of your biases. It is common for younger teachers to undervalue years of experience, and it is common for older teachers to overvalue years of experience.
The best path is not to judge someone based on how long they've been teaching, but rather on the results their work produces.
Some teachers balk at being expected to attend to so much in every child, but such is the high call of long-term flourishing.
So, for my younger colleagues, be humble! Set your face like flint on putting in the work over the long haul. And for my older colleagues, be humble, too!

Finally, keep asking yourself: What kind of experience am I building today? If we build the right kind — the kind filled with warm self-critique, humble-boldness, and the focused pursuit of excellence in six key areas — and if we do this year in and year out, then we're going to arrive at a place where the work is consistently rewarding.
